questions.q: What is the real difference between a fixed-size and a dynamic array in Solidity?
options: A fixed-size array (like uint[5]) is locked to that many entries forever; a dynamic array (uint[]) can grow
Dynamic arrays are always faster and cheaper than fixed-size arrays
There is no real difference — the syntax is identical
Fixed-size arrays can hold unlimited items
questions.explain: uint[5] numbers locks the array to exactly 5 entries, while uint[] public numbers has no fixed size and grows as items are pushed to it.

questions.q: In the egg-carton analogy from this lesson, if you have six eggs, what index does the first egg have?
options: 0, since array indexes always start at zero
There is no index for the first item
questions.explain: Array indexes always start at zero — six eggs occupy indexes 0 through 5, not 1 through 6.

questions.q: What does `numbers.push(1)` actually do to a real array?
options: Adds the value 1 to the end of the array
Removes the first item from the array
Replaces every item in the array with 1
questions.explain: push adds a new value to the end of a dynamic array, growing its length by one.

questions.q: What is an enum, per this lesson?
options: A user-defined type that assigns names to a set of integer values, improving clarity and safety
A type that can only ever hold true or false
A keyword used only inside constructors
questions.explain: An enum, like `enum Status { Pending, Shipped, Delivered }`, gives real names to a fixed set of underlying integer values.

questions.q: Why is `status = Status.Shipped;` considered safer than assigning a raw number like `1`?
options: The named value is unambiguous and can't accidentally be set to an invalid number outside the defined set
Raw numbers are actually always safer in Solidity
Enums and raw numbers behave completely differently at runtime
There's no real safety benefit — it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: Using the named enum value avoids the ambiguity and risk of raw "magic numbers," since Status.Shipped can only ever refer to one of the enum's defined states.
